seo_title: ElectraSim Guide — Circuits, Faults, Smart Wiring and Guided Templates
seo_description: Learn the current ElectraSim workflow: guided circuit templates, smart and custom wiring, fault simulation, import/export, alignment tools, mini-map, and eight step-by-step wiring walkthroughs.
hero_heading:
Build Real Circuits.
Learn by Simulating.
hero_description: A practical guide to the current ElectraSim app: start with guided templates, wire circuits with smart or custom routing, test faults, organise large diagrams, and practise eight real wiring walkthroughs.
cta_heading: You know the current workflow. Now build your own circuit.
cta_description: Use guided templates, fault mode, smart routing, custom wiring, and export tools for free in your browser. No sign-up, no installation.

latest_features.title: Guided Circuit Templates
latest_features.body: Open 18 built-in guided circuits straight inside the app: eight starter circuits (lamps, one-way and two-way switching, RCD fault checks, contactors, timers, a push-button doorbell, an RCBO socket) and ten Pro scenarios — three-phase motor control, EV charging, solar with battery storage, underfloor heating, staircase timers, PIR floodlights, cooker supplies, surge-protected consumer units, generator backup and AFDD bedrooms.

latest_features.title: Fault Simulation Mode
latest_features.body: Inject wire breaks, reverse polarity, and missing-earth faults directly on the canvas, then compare the warning and error feedback.

latest_features.title: Smart and Custom Wiring
latest_features.body: Use default smart right-angle routing around components, or enable custom wiring to place manual checkpoint corners for real cable-run teaching.

latest_features.title: Import, Export and Share
latest_features.body: Export circuits as JSON, SVG, PNG, PDF/print sheets, or shareable URLs. Import is schema-validated so broken files do not corrupt your work.

latest_features.title: Canvas Organisation Tools
latest_features.body: Use drag-select, copy/paste, alignment, distribution, mini-map navigation, zoom-to-fit, gridless mode, and colour presets for larger diagrams.

latest_features.title: Performance and Accessibility
latest_features.body: Choose light, dark, or system theme, high-contrast and colour-blind canvas palettes, and reduced visual effects for lower-powered devices.

circuits.title: Protected Lamp Circuit
circuits.description: The shortest complete circuit here: a supply, one protective device and a lamp, with nothing to switch it. Build this first — every other walkthrough is this path with something added.
steps: Place a Live (L) terminal and a Neutral (N) terminal on the canvas.
Place an MCB to the right of the Live terminal.
Place a Bulb (E27) to the right of the MCB.
Wire: Live → MCB → Bulb → Neutral.
Press Run, then select the bulb and read its voltage and current in the Inspector.
Toggle the MCB off and run again — the lamp goes dark because the live feed is gone, not because the neutral moved.
circuits.insight: A lamp needs both rails: a live feed and a neutral return. The MCB sits in the live conductor only, so opening it removes the feed while the neutral path stays connected back to the supply.

circuits.title: Single-Lamp Switched Circuit
circuits.description: The most fundamental circuit in household wiring. A switch in series controls one bulb. This is the exact wiring behind every ceiling light.
steps: Place a Live (L) terminal and a Neutral (N) terminal on the canvas.
Place an MCB to the right of the Live terminal.
Place a Single-way Switch to the right of the MCB.
Place a Bulb (E27) to the right of the Switch.
Wire: Live → MCB → Switch → Bulb → Neutral.
Press Run. Toggle the Switch to turn the bulb on and off.
circuits.insight: The MCB is always wired in series — it protects the entire circuit. The switch interrupts only the Live wire, keeping Neutral permanently connected back to supply.

circuits.title: Two-Bulb Parallel Circuit
circuits.description: Wire two bulbs in parallel so each receives full voltage independently. This is how all household lighting and sockets are wired — one bulb failing or being removed has no effect on the other.
circuits.diagram:
Live → MCB → Switch → Junction Box → Bulb A
                                        → Bulb B → Neutral
steps: Build the single-lamp circuit from Circuit 1.
Add a Junction Box after the Switch.
Place a second Bulb below the first.
Wire the Junction Box output to both bulbs.
Connect both Bulb Neutral ports back to the Neutral terminal.
Press Run — both bulbs light at full brightness.
Disconnect one bulb wire — the other stays on. That's parallel wiring.
circuits.insight: In a parallel circuit, every branch receives the full supply voltage. Adding more branches increases total current drawn — the MCB protects against overload if too many loads are connected.

circuits.title: Two-Way Switching (Staircase Circuit)
circuits.description: Control one light from two separate locations — the classic staircase or hallway circuit. Switch the light on upstairs, switch it off downstairs, and vice versa.
circuits.diagram:
Live → MCB → SW1 COM
SW1 L1 ——→ SW2 L1 (strapping)
SW1 L2 ——→ SW2 L2 (strapping)
SW2 COM → Bulb → Neutral
steps: Place Live, Neutral, MCB, and a Bulb.
Place two Two-way Switches between the MCB and the Bulb.
Wire MCB → Switch 1 COM port.
Wire Switch 1 L1 → Switch 2 L1 (first strapping wire).
Wire Switch 1 L2 → Switch 2 L2 (second strapping wire).
Wire Switch 2 COM → Bulb.
Wire Bulb Neutral → Neutral terminal.
Press Run. Toggle either switch — the bulb responds from both locations.
circuits.insight: Two-way switching works because the two strapping wires always form exactly one complete path — toggling either switch swaps which wire is connected, turning the circuit on or off.

circuits.title: RCD-Protected Socket Circuit
circuits.description: Add earth fault protection to a socket outlet using an RCD. This is mandatory in bathrooms, kitchens, and outdoor circuits in modern installations.
circuits.diagram:
Live → MCB → RCD (L-in→L-out) → Socket (L)
Neutral → RCD (N-in→N-out) → Socket (N)
Earth → Socket (E)
steps: Place Live, Neutral, and Earth terminals.
Place an MCB and wire Live → MCB.
Place an RCD. Wire MCB output → RCD L-in. Wire Neutral → RCD N-in.
Place a 3-Pin Socket.
Wire RCD L-out → Socket L.
Wire RCD N-out → Socket N.
Wire Earth terminal → Socket E.
Press Run — the socket is live and protected by both the MCB and RCD.
circuits.insight: The RCD monitors the difference between Live and Neutral current. Any leakage (e.g. through a person to earth) causes an imbalance and trips the RCD in under 40ms — far faster than an MCB and before lethal harm can occur.

circuits.title: Timed Outdoor Lighting
circuits.description: Automate an outdoor light to turn on and off at set times using a Timer Switch — no manual intervention required once programmed.
circuits.diagram: Live → MCB → Timer Switch → Bulb → Neutral
steps: Place Live, Neutral, MCB, a Timer Switch, and a Bulb.
Wire: Live → MCB → Timer Switch (L-in) → Timer Switch (L-out) → Bulb → Neutral.
Press Run. The circuit is live.
Click the Timer Switch to simulate it reaching its ON trigger time — the bulb activates.
Click again to simulate the OFF time — the bulb goes dark.
circuits.insight: A Timer Switch is just a switch with an internal clock mechanism. In ElectraSim you toggle it manually to represent time events. In a real installation, the timer's ON/OFF schedule is programmed with physical pegs or a digital interface.

circuits.title: Dimmable Lighting Circuit
circuits.description: Add a Dimmer Switch to a lighting circuit for variable brightness control. Use this for living rooms, dining rooms, and any space where ambience matters.
circuits.diagram: Live → MCB → Dimmer Switch → Bulb → Neutral
steps: Place Live, Neutral, MCB, a Dimmer Switch, and a Bulb.
Wire: Live → MCB → Dimmer (L-in) → Dimmer (L-out) → Bulb → Neutral.
Press Run — the bulb is powered through the dimmer.
Toggle the Dimmer to see the controlled state.
circuits.insight: In real installations, a dimmer switch must be matched to the bulb type — trailing-edge for LED, leading-edge for incandescent/halogen. Never connect a Dimmer Switch to a motor or fan (use a Fan Dimmer instead).

circuits.title: Doorbell Circuit
circuits.description: Build the classic doorbell: a Push Button (momentary switch) in series with a Bell/Buzzer. The bell sounds only while the button is held — exactly like a real doorbell.
circuits.diagram: Live → MCB → Push Button → Bell → Neutral
steps: Place Live, Neutral, MCB, a Push Button, and a Bell/Buzzer.
Wire: Live → MCB → Push Button (L-in → L-out) → Bell (L) → Neutral (N).
Press Run.
Click and hold the Push Button — the Bell activates.
Release the button — the Bell stops. That's a momentary circuit.
circuits.insight: Push Buttons are momentary — they close the circuit only while physically held. A standard switch latches open or closed. This distinction is critical: a latching switch would leave the bell ringing continuously.

circuits.title: Timer-Controlled Bell
circuits.description: A bell or buzzer on a timed contact. The timer switch is an ordinary switch driven by a clock, which is why the bell sounds for a set period and then stops on its own.
circuits.diagram: Live → MCB → Timer Switch → Bell → Neutral
steps: Place a Live (L) terminal and a Neutral (N) terminal on the canvas.
Place an MCB on the live side, then a Timer Switch to its right.
Place a Bell as the load.
Wire: Live → MCB → Timer Switch → Bell → Neutral.
Press Run, then toggle the timer switch to stand in for the timed contact closing and opening.
Select the timer in the Inspector to compare its weekly, staircase and countdown variants.
circuits.insight: A timer switch is a switch with a clock attached: it closes the live conductor for a set interval, then opens it. A bell is an intermittent load, so the timer is what stops it being left energised.

circuits.title: RCBO-Protected Socket
circuits.description: A socket outlet fed through an RCBO, with its protective earth run straight from the earth terminal and a lamp standing in for a plugged-in appliance. One device covers both overcurrent and earth-leakage protection for the whole circuit.
circuits.diagram:
Live + Neutral → RCBO → Socket → Bulb (test load)
Earth → Socket (E)
steps: Place Live (L), Neutral (N) and Earth (E) terminals down the left of the canvas.
Place an RCBO between the supply and the socket.
Wire Live and Neutral into the RCBO at L-in and N-in.
Take L-out and N-out from the RCBO to the socket's L and N terminals.
Run Earth straight to the socket's E terminal — it must not pass through the RCBO.
Feed a test lamp from the socket's Live and Neutral, then press Run.
Open the RCBO: both outgoing conductors are interrupted while Earth stays connected.
circuits.insight: An RCBO breaks live and neutral together, so an open device leaves the socket dead on both rails. Earth never passes through it — a protective conductor that can be switched is not a protective conductor.

circuits.title: Contactor Motor Starter
circuits.description: A motor branch switched by a contactor. The MCB protects the cable, the contactor does the switching, and it breaks live and neutral together so the motor is isolated when the coil drops out.
steps: Place a Live (L) terminal and a Neutral (N) terminal on the canvas.
Place an MCB on the live conductor to protect the cable.
Place a Contactor after the MCB, then a Motor as the load.
Wire Live → MCB → Contactor, and Neutral → Contactor.
Take the contactor's switched live and switched neutral through to the motor.
Press Run, then toggle the contactor or the MCB — either one stops the motor.
circuits.insight: Protection and switching are separate jobs: the MCB clears overcurrent while the contactor handles the repeated making and breaking of an inductive load. Switching both conductors means the motor is never left sitting on a live rail when the contactor drops out.

circuits.title: Full Consumer Unit (3-Circuit Panel)
circuits.description: Build a complete home breaker panel using a Distribution Board. Three independent circuits — lighting, sockets, and a motor — each protected by their own MCB.
circuits.diagram:
Live → DB (L-in) → L1 → MCB1 → Switch → Bulb
                    → L2 → MCB2 → 3-Pin Socket
                    → L3 → MCB3 → Motor
Neutral → DB (N-in) → N1/N2 → (all returns)
steps: Place a Live terminal, Neutral terminal, and a Distribution Board.
Wire: Live → DB L-in. Wire: Neutral → DB N-in.
Circuit 1 (Lighting): DB L1 → MCB1 → Switch → Bulb → DB N1.
Circuit 2 (Sockets): DB L2 → MCB2 → 3-Pin Socket (L) → DB N1.
Circuit 3 (Motor): DB L3 → MCB3 → Motor (L) → DB N2.
Press Run — all three circuits operate independently.
Trip MCB2 — only the socket goes dead. Lighting and motor stay running.
circuits.insight: The key principle of a consumer unit is circuit isolation: a fault on one circuit trips only that MCB, leaving all other circuits unaffected. This is why each circuit has its own dedicated breaker.
